summary: Risalah refers to the divine institution of prophethood — Allah's selection of human messengers to convey His guidance to mankind. Belief in all prophets and messengers is among the six articles of faith.
content:
Risalah (prophethood and messengership) is a divine mercy: Allah did not leave humanity without guidance. Throughout history, He sent prophets and messengers to every people, conveying the same essential message — worship Allah alone — while the specific laws they brought varied according to time and community.

Allah says: 'And We certainly sent into every nation a messenger, saying: Worship Allah and avoid false deities' (16:36). This universality of prophethood is a fundamental element of Islamic belief.

## Prophets and Messengers: The Distinction

Classical scholars distinguish between a nabi (prophet) and a rasul (messenger). A nabi is one who receives revelation but conveys an existing law, while a rasul is one sent with a new law or primary message to a community. All messengers are prophets, but not all prophets are messengers. The distinction carries theological weight but does not affect the obligation to believe in all of them.

## The Named Prophets

The Quran mentions twenty-five prophets by name. They are: Adam, Idris (Enoch), Nuh (Noah), Hud, Salih, Ibrahim (Abraham), Lut (Lot), Ismail (Ishmael), Ishaq (Isaac), Yaqub (Jacob), Yusuf (Joseph), Shu'ayb, Musa (Moses), Harun (Aaron), Dhul-Kifl (possibly Ezekiel), Dawud (David), Sulayman (Solomon), Ilyas (Elijah), al-Yasa' (Elisha), Yunus (Jonah), Zakariyya (Zechariah), Yahya (John), Isa (Jesus), and Muhammad (peace be upon them all).

The Quran also indicates that there were many prophets not mentioned by name: 'And there are messengers about whom We have told you before, and messengers about whom We have not told you' (4:164). The number commonly cited in hadith is 124,000 prophets, though the chain of this specific narration requires scholarly examination.

## The Finality of Prophethood (Khatm al-Nubuwwah)

Muhammad (peace be upon him) is the last and final prophet. This is established beyond doubt in the Quran: 'Muhammad is not the father of any of your men, but he is the Messenger of Allah and the last (khatam) of the prophets' (33:40). The Prophet himself said: 'There is no prophet after me' (Bukhari 3455, Muslim 1842).

The finality of prophethood means that the revelation is complete. The Quran and authenticated Sunnah constitute the final and preserved divine guidance for humanity until the Day of Judgement. No new revelation, new prophet, or new religion can supersede or add to what was brought by Muhammad (peace be upon him).

The Ahmadiyya movement's claim that Mirza Ghulam Ahmad was a prophet after Muhammad is rejected by the scholarly consensus of all Muslim communities as a nullifier of Islam. This is one of the few matters where near-unanimous scholarly agreement exists.

## Qualities of the Prophets

Classical scholars enumerated four essential qualities that all prophets share:

1. **Sidq (Truthfulness)** — they never lie
2. **Amanah (Trustworthiness)** — they never betray
3. **Tabligh (Conveyance)** — they fully deliver the message entrusted to them
4. **Fatanah (Intelligence)** — they possess the wisdom and understanding to fulfill their mission

The opposite of each quality is impossible for prophets: they cannot lie, betray, conceal the message, or be foolish.

## The Role of Prophet Muhammad (Peace Be Upon Him)

Muhammad (peace be upon him) was sent not just to one people but to all of humanity and jinn: 'And We have not sent you except as a mercy to the worlds' (21:107). His Sunnah — his words, actions, and tacit approvals — is the second source of Islamic law and the lived interpretation of the Quran.

Belief in his prophethood is inseparable from the shahada. To accept tawhid without accepting his messengership is not Islam. The shahada — 'La ilaha illallah, Muhammadur rasulullah' — joins both pillars in a single declaration.

## Believing in All Prophets

A Muslim must believe in all prophets without distinction of rank in terms of obligation to accept them. Allah says: 'The Messenger has believed in what was revealed to him from his Lord, and the believers. All of them have believed in Allah and His angels and His books and His messengers, saying: We make no distinction between any of His messengers' (2:285). Rejecting any prophet, or claiming that a later religion superseded the obligation to follow Muhammad, is kufr.
evidence_quran: Surah an-Nahl 16:36 — 'And We certainly sent into every nation a messenger, saying: Worship Allah and avoid false deities'
Surah al-Ahzab 33:40 — 'Muhammad is not the father of any of your men, but he is the Messenger of Allah and the last of the prophets'
Surah an-Nisa 4:164 — 'And there are messengers about whom We have told you before, and messengers about whom We have not told you'
Surah al-Anbiya 21:107 — 'And We have not sent you except as a mercy to the worlds'
Surah al-Baqarah 2:285 — 'We make no distinction between any of His messengers'
evidence_hadith: Bukhari 3455, Muslim 1842 — 'There is no prophet after me'
Muslim 523 — 'I was given five things which were not given to anyone before me...' (universality of the Prophet's mission)
Ahmad (with strong chains) — prophets number 124,000 (chain requires scholarly verification)
scholar_positions: The finality of prophethood (khatm al-nubuwwah) is held by scholarly ijma'. The Ahmadiyya claim to prophethood is rejected by consensus. The specific distinction between nabi and rasul is discussed by classical scholars including Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Qayyim; the details are technical but the obligation to believe in all prophets is agreed upon across all schools.
sources: Ibn Kathir, Tafsir al-Quran al-Azim (commentary on 33:40 and 21:107)
Ibn al-Qayyim, Zad al-Ma'ad (biography and prophethood of Muhammad)
al-Nawawi, Sharh Muslim (commentary on hadith of finality)
al-Tahawiyyah al-Aqeedah — Imam al-Tahawi (d. 321 AH), with commentary by Ibn Abi al-Izz
